benign, stable, isolated mild thrombocytopenia - not ITP.

ITP is by definition platelet <100k, diagnosis of exclusion,
isolated thrombocytopenia with normal smear, normal other
counts, no splenomegaly, no liver disease, no drugs,
no infection, no autoimmune disease, no inherited giant-platelet
disorder, no pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA clumping.

Here:

* 4 years stable 100-150k, now 110k
* no bleeding except for the index postpartum hemorrhage
which brought her to count - i.e. detection bias
* no liver disease, no splenomegaly / hypersplenism
* no transfusions / alloimmunization
* no family history of inherited thrombocytopenia
* normal hemoglobin, WBC, differential, creatinine, no hemolysis,
no renal failure to suggest TTP/HUS, aplasia, MDS, leukemia
* asymptomatic

That course predicts a benign course. Most borderline
100-150k remain stable, do not progress to <50k or to
severe bleeding or to systemic autoimmune disease, and
110k is hemostatically adequate.

110k requires no hemostatic therapy and no diagnostic
bone marrow procedure:

* no prophylactic platelet transfusion
* no corticosteroids, IVIG, anti-D, rituximab,
  thrombopoietin-receptor agonist, immunosuppression
* no splenectomy
* no bone marrow biopsy for stable isolated mild
  thrombocytopenia with normal smear and normal other lines

In particular in a child-bearing age woman avoid
unnecessary platelet transfusion and alloimmunization
unless life-threatening bleeding.

Assuming true thrombocytopenia is confirmed once by
peripheral smear - no clumps, no satellitism, no giant
platelets missed by the auto-counter - and medication,
alcohol, pregnancy, HIV, HCV, thyroid disease review
is negative:

reassure, bleeding precautions, and watchful waiting.

* routine CBC e.g. every 6-12 mo, sooner in pregnancy,
  illness, new drugs, bleeding, surgery
* avoid NSAIDs, excess alcohol, thrombocytopenic drugs
* no restriction for most surgery - >50k adequate for
  most procedures, >70-80k adequate for delivery and
  neuraxial anesthesia
* re-evaluate to hematology if: fall to <100k and
  persistent, <30k, bleeding, other cytopenia,
  lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, autoimmune symptoms

Treatment of ITP is to prevent bleeding, not to normalize
the count, and is indicated only for <20-30k, bleeding,
or high-risk procedure.

No - hemoglobinopathy work-up is not indicated here, and would be low-yield and potentially misleading.

This is severe, confirmed iron deficiency anemia with a refractory course that needs cause-of-iron-loss/malabsorption work-up and effective repletion, not thalassemia/sickle work-up.

**Why this is iron deficiency, not thalassemia:**

Microcytic hypochromic differential: iron deficiency, thalassemia trait, anemia of chronic disease/inflammation, sideroblastic anemia, lead poisoning, copper deficiency.

Here you have:
- Hgb 7.3 g/dL, MCV 67 fL, hypochromia + microcytosis
- ferritin <5 ng/mL + low iron saturation

Ferritin <15 ng/mL in an adult is essentially diagnostic of iron deficiency, <5 is unequivocal even with inflammation. Anemia of chronic disease has normal/high ferritin. Thalassemia trait has normal to high ferritin, normal RDW, normal/high RBC count, mild anemia - typically Hgb 9-11, MCV 65-75, lifelong, often with family history and ethnic predisposition.

A 52-year-old otherwise healthy woman with no family history presenting for the first time with severe symptomatic anemia Hgb 7.3 is not thalassemia trait or intermedia. Trait does not cause Hgb 7.3, fatigue of recent onset, or ferritin <5. Coexistent trait + iron deficiency is possible, but you cannot diagnose it now and it does not explain this presentation.

Importantly, iron deficiency lowers HbA2, so hemoglobin electrophoresis/HPLC done now can falsely mask beta-thalassemia trait. Defer any such testing until iron replete, and only if microcytosis persists despite repletion, RBC count is disproportionately high, RDW normal, Mentzer index <13, or suggestive family/ethnic history.

Cats, recurrent dysuria/pyridium use do not suggest hemoglobinopathy. Phenazopyridine can cause oxidative hemolysis/methemoglobinemia, especially in G6PD deficiency or renal failure, but that is normocytic with Heinz bodies/bite cells, reticulocytosis, normal ferritin - not severe microcytic hypochromic anemia with absent stores.

**What she needs: refractory iron deficiency work-up**

Intermittent oral iron "failure" is common and does not equal refractory disease. Clarify adherence, dose of elemental iron, frequency, tolerance, inhibitors - tea/coffee, calcium, antacids/PPI, levothyroxine - and ongoing loss.

History needed:
menstrual status at 52 - still cycling, menorrhagia, postmenopausal bleeding, pregnancies, fibroids; GI - melena, hematochezia, hematemesis, dyspepsia, dysphagia, weight loss, bowel change, NSAIDs, anticoagulant/antiplatelet, prior bariatric surgery, PPI use, diet/vegetarian, pica/pagophagia, restless legs, hair loss, blood donation; urinary - true infection vs hematuria, stones, incontinence products masking bleeding; full meds, alcohol, weight, vitals, pallor, cheilitis, koilonychia, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly.

Labs/exam now:
CBC with diff/platelets, RBC count, RDW, retic count, repeat iron panel/ferritin, B12/folate, CMP, CRP/ESR, TSH, celiac screen tTG-IgA + total IgA, stool FIT/guaiac x3, urinalysis with microscopy + urine culture - do not rely on dipstick on pyridium, orange dye interferes. Stop masking recurrent urinary symptoms with intermittent phenazopyridine alone - treat cause.

Age >50, post/perimenopausal, Hgb 7.3 with no obvious menstrual cause = bidirectional endoscopy per AGA/ACG: EGD + colonoscopy to rule out GI blood loss/malignancy, celiac disease, H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, angiodysplasia. Gynecology input if abnormal uterine bleeding. Urology if persistent hematuria.

Management:
1. Optimize iron: e.g. ferrous sulfate 325mg ~65mg elemental iron daily or alternate-day on empty stomach with vitamin C, separate from calcium/antacids/tea/coffee. Expect Hgb rise ~1-2 g/dL in 4-6 weeks, continue 3 months after normalization to replete stores. Counsel constipation, nausea, dark stools.
2. Given Hgb 7.3 and prior oral failure, low threshold for IV iron - e.g. ferric carboxymaltose, iron dextran - especially if intolerant, malabsorption, ongoing loss, need for rapid repletion. Transfuse only for hemodynamic instability, ischemic symptoms, not for number alone.
3. Treat underlying loss source found on GI/GU work-up, eradicate H. pylori if positive, treat celiac if found.

Only reconsider thalassemia/hemoglobinopathy if after adequate repletion and exclusion of blood loss, MCV remains <70-75 with normal ferritin, elevated RBC count, normal RDW.

In this asymptomatic 45 year old, persistent FIT positivity
cannot be deferred to the 5-year post-polypectomy date.

He is now in colonoscopy surveillance, not FIT screening,
and needs prompt diagnostic colonoscopy - despite a
colonoscopy ~12 months ago with complete removal of
1 hyperplastic polyp and 2 adenomas <1 cm.

Reasoning:

1. **FIT is a screening test for asymptomatic average-risk
adults, not a work-up for diarrhea.** The initial FIT done
for prolonged diarrhea after international travel was
inappropriate. Acute infectious enterocolitis, inflammatory
diarrhea, hemorrhoids, fissure, NSAIDs can cause transient
FIT positivity.

That does not apply now. He is asymptomatic with diarrhea
resolved, and has **2 positive FITs ~5 months apart,
~7 and ~12 months after colonoscopy**. Persistent positivity
when asymptomatic greatly increases positive predictive value
for colorectal blood loss and cannot be attributed to
traveler's diarrhea.

FIT detects intact human globin. It is largely degraded
from upper GI/small bowel. A positive FIT is lower GI,
essentially colorectal until proven otherwise.

2. **Recent colonoscopy does not rule out neoplasia.**
Miss rates in high-quality colonoscopy are ~20-25% for
adenomas overall, ~5-10% for advanced adenomas, higher
for right-sided, flat and serrated lesions. Incomplete
resection/recurrence at polypectomy sites, inadequate prep,
incomplete exam, short withdrawal also occur.

Two <10mm tubular adenomas completely removed = low-risk
adenomas. One <10mm hyperplastic polyp = non-neoplastic
for surveillance purposes. They do not explain ongoing
bleeding 1 year later, and complete removal does not
protect against a missed synchronous lesion or rapidly
missed lesion.

In other words: do not use the 1-year-ago "reassuring"
colonoscopy and the 5-year recommendation to ignore
new objective bleeding.

US Multi-Society, ACG, USPSTF: any positive FIT in an
average-risk adult requires colonoscopy, promptly,
typically within 2-3 months. Persistent double positivity
is an even stronger indication. Do not repeat FIT,
do not do FIT for post-polypectomy surveillance, do not
substitute flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonography,
and do not do routine upper endoscopy for isolated
FIT positivity without upper symptoms or iron-deficiency
anemia.

3. **Distractors do not change risk:**
- Mother with osteoarthritis at 65 = no family history
of colorectal cancer, adenoma, or polyposis syndrome.
He is average risk for family history, but average risk
with positive FIT still needs colonoscopy.
- Age 45 is now screening-start age, but he is already
in surveillance because of adenomas. Surveillance is
by colonoscopy at interval, not by annual FIT.

Recommended evaluation:

- Refer to gastroenterology for colonoscopy now, not in
5 years. Review prior colonoscopy quality before repeat:
indication, bowel prep score, cecal intubation with photo,
withdrawal time, adenoma detection, resection technique
and completeness, location of polyps for site re-examination.
- History: rectal bleeding, hemorrhoids, fissure, change
in bowel habit, weight loss, abdominal pain, NSAID,
antiplatelet, anticoagulant use, CKD, IBD symptoms.
Med review, rectal exam, CBC/ferritin for anemia, but
absence of anemia or hemorrhoids does not obviate
colonoscopy. Do not attribute persistent FIT positivity
to hemorrhoids without looking.
- High-quality repeat colonoscopy with split-dose prep,
careful inspection including prior polypectomy sites,
right colon and serrated pathway.

If repeat high-quality complete colonoscopy is negative
with no advanced neoplasia, then stop FIT screening and
return to colonoscopy surveillance. Interval is then
reset from the most recent high-quality exam - per
2020 USMSTF 1-2 tubular adenomas <10mm would be 7-10
years, local practice often 5 years; individualize with
gastroenterology given two exams in 1 year.

No - do not empirically restart indefinite anticoagulation now for a 3.5 year old, treated, isolated subsegmental PE that has remained event-free off therapy.

This is not a standard proximal unprovoked PE where indefinite therapy is favored in a low-bleed patient. The index event, the timing, and this patient change the benefit-harm calculation.

**1. The index event was isolated subsegmental PE, not proximal PE/DVT.**

Isolated subsegmental PE of the right lower lobe, treated with 3 months of apixaban, with no recurrence in 3.5 years off anticoagulation:

* False positive CT, artifact, and low clinical significance are much more common with single subsegmental defects than with lobar, segmental, multiple subsegmental, or proximal disease. Diagnosis should be verified by review of the original CT and documentation of bilateral lower extremity ultrasound at the time. If there was concomitant proximal DVT, management is as proximal VTE - but isolated subsegmental without DVT is different.
* Recurrence risk after isolated subsegmental PE without DVT and without ongoing major risk factor is substantially lower than after unprovoked proximal PE/DVT.
* ASH 2020 and CHEST 2021 for VTE management both make a conditional recommendation for this exact phenotype:

> For isolated subsegmental PE with no proximal DVT in the legs, clinical surveillance is suggested over anticoagulation when there is low risk of recurrent VTE, and anticoagulation is suggested when there is high risk of recurrence - e.g. hospitalized, reduced mobility, active cancer, prior VTE, concomitant DVT.

In other words, unprovoked does not automatically = indefinite when the clot burden is isolated subsegmental. Initial 3 months of apixaban was appropriate definitive therapy for the acute event.

Even for truly unprovoked proximal VTE, guidelines recommend the decision for extended/indefinite therapy be made at completion of the initial 3-6 months after assessing recurrence risk vs bleeding risk, not years later.

**2. 3.5 years event-free off anticoagulation is highly informative.**

Recurrence risk after stopping for unprovoked VTE is front-loaded - highest in the first 6-12 months after stopping. She has now passed that high-risk window with:

* no new clotting events
* no ongoing signs of VTE
* no family history of VTE
* age-appropriate malignancy screening negative, no active cancer
* stable CBC, metabolic panel

Her observed phenotype is now low recurrence, not high recurrence. Late re-initiation of therapeutic anticoagulation without a new thrombus, new persistent major risk factor such as active cancer, antiphospholipid syndrome, recurrent unprovoked VTE, or high-risk thrombophilia, is not supported and exposes her to bleeding without proven benefit.

Routine D-dimer, serial ultrasounds, or inherited thrombophilia testing 3.5 years later will not change this decision and are not recommended in the absence of family history, recurrent events, or clot in unusual site. Ferritin 1059 ng/mL stable in an ESRD/transplant patient most often reflects transfusion history, inflammation, CKD, liver disease - evaluate separately, but it is not a prothrombotic indication for anticoagulation.

**3. Bleeding risk in a kidney transplant recipient is not low.**

Deceased-donor transplant a few years ago implies:

* chronic kidney disease even with functioning graft, anemia, uremic platelet dysfunction history
* immunosuppression - corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, antimetabolites - with thrombocytopenia, anemia, hypertension, liver/kidney fluctuation, infection risk
* drug interactions: apixaban is P-gp and CYP3A4 substrate. Cyclosporine in particular increases apixaban exposure via P-gp inhibition; tacrolimus, azoles, and other transplant drugs add variability.
* concomitant antiplatelet, NSAID use, fall/trauma consequences living alone

Formal bleeding assessment - hemoglobin/platelets, creatinine/eGFR and liver function trends, blood pressure control, alcohol, NSAIDs, antiplatelets, fall history, prior bleeding on apixaban, VTE-BLEED/HAS-BLED type factors - is required before any consideration of indefinite therapy. In this patient net harm likely exceeds net benefit.

Living alone in a single-story home with cats is functionally favorable - no stairs, independent - but does not create an indication for anticoagulation, and living alone increases hazard of an unrecognized bleed.

What to do instead:

1. Do not restart therapeutic apixaban/warfarin. Document shared decision-making.
2. Verify history: review original CT report/images, confirm no proximal DVT, confirm 3-month course completed, confirm no interval VTE, bleeding, or new risk factor.
3. Continue age-appropriate cancer screening, transplant surveillance, BP, lipids, smoking, activity, weight optimization.
4. Counsel on VTE symptoms and need for prompt evaluation, and on situational prophylaxis - hospitalization, surgery, prolonged immobilization, long travel, estrogen therapy which should be avoided. Use guideline-based prophylaxis at those times, not continuous therapy.
5. No routine hematology referral required solely for this remote event unless new concern, but referral is reasonable if diagnostic uncertainty or patient anxiety.
6. Reassess only if new VTE, active cancer, major persistent risk factor develops, or high-risk surgery/transplant dysfunction.

In short: a remote, treated, isolated unprovoked subsegmental PE with 3.5 years of stability off therapy, no active cancer or recurrence, in a stable transplant recipient, should be managed with observation, not late indefinite anticoagulation.

No - testing is not indicated right now.

This is a diagnostic stewardship issue. Do not test for *C. difficile* based on loose stool alone in a low pre-test probability patient.

IDSA 2017/2021 *C. difficile* guidelines target testing to:

> unexplained new-onset **≥3 unformed stools in 24 hours**

Do not test formed stool, do not test asymptomatic patients, do not test as test-of-cure, and do not test when there is a clear alternative explanation for diarrhea.

This patient does not meet that:

1. **No clinically significant diarrhea as defined:** persistent loose stool, but specifically no watery stool, and no stated frequency of ≥3 unformed stools/24hr, no abdominal cramping/pain, no fever, chills, leukocytosis, AKI. Loose non-watery, painless, afebrile stool is not classic for *C. difficile* infection.

2. **Atypical presentation for CDI:** CDI is typically acute watery, non-bloody diarrhea with crampy lower abdominal pain, fever, leukocytosis, often with recent high-risk antibiotics, hospitalization, age >65, PPI use, chemotherapy.
Gross bloody stool is uncommon in CDI. Bloody stool suggests infectious colitis - Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, EHEC - IBD, ischemia, etc. Her bloody stools have resolved, which argues further against active CDI colitis now.

3. **Clear alternative explanations:**
- atypical pneumonia itself: Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila can present with pneumonia + diarrhea, nausea, abdominal upset.
- azithromycin side effect: macrolides commonly cause nausea, loose stools, antibiotic-associated osmotic diarrhea. Azithromycin is low-risk for CDI compared to clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, broad-spectrum cephalosporins and penicillins.

4. **High risk of false positive from colonization:**
History of prior CDI treated with fecal microbiota transplant is a risk factor for recurrence, and antibiotics can trigger recurrence, so vigilance is appropriate. But FMT recipients can remain colonized with *C. difficile* by highly sensitive NAAT without toxin-mediated disease.

Testing a low-probability patient with NAAT alone detects colonization, not infection, leading to unnecessary vancomycin/fidaxomicin, further microbiome disruption, VRE selection, cost, and missed true diagnosis. That is why labs reject formed stool and require unformed stool that takes the shape of the container.

Mother with diverticulosis at 72 is a distractor - age-related, low-fiber associated, not a CDI risk factor.

What to do instead:

- Get a stool diary: number/24hr, Bristol type 1-7, duration, urgency, incontinence, diet, laxatives, PPI, other antibiotics, hospitalization, sick contacts, travel.
- Vitals, exam, CBC, creatinine - look for fever, leukocytosis, AKI that would raise suspicion.
- Supportive care, hydration, avoid anti-motility agents if colitis suspected, review need for ongoing antibiotics and PPI, do not give probiotics to prevent CDI outside trial.
- Do not send stool culture, ova/parasites, calprotectin now unless indicated by new symptoms.

Re-evaluate and test with a multi-step algorithm - GDH + toxin EIA with NAAT arbitration - **if** she develops:
≥3 unformed/watery stools in 24hr unexplained by laxatives, plus cramping, fever, leukocytosis, especially within 30 days of antibiotics/hospitalization.

If bloody stools recur, pursue non-CDI workup: infectious stool workup, fecal calprotectin, GI referral for IBD, ischemic colitis, microscopic colitis evaluation, not isolated CDI testing.

This is educational information only and not medical advice for a specific patient - this patient needs in-person evaluation with sexual health / ID and OB-GYN.

### Is PEP indicated if the single exposure was >72 hours ago?

No.

For non-occupational HIV exposure from receptive vaginal intercourse with a partner with HIV who is likely viremic - recently diagnosed, presumably not yet virally suppressed on ART:

* PEP is recommended only if started as soon as possible and **no later than 72 hours after exposure**, for 28 days.
* There is no demonstrated efficacy after 72 hours, and toxicity, cost, drug interactions, and risk of resistance if acute infection is already established outweigh any theoretical benefit.
* CDC, WHO, and DHHS nPEP guidelines: **do not prescribe PEP if >72 hours** since exposure.

Important history to clarify before closing the decision:

1. Exact timing of exposure - single exposure vs ongoing exposures. If there was *another* unprotected exposure within the last 72 hours, PEP would be considered for that most recent exposure.
2. Source details if available with consent: time of HIV diagnosis, on ART or not, most recent viral load, CD4, resistance genotype, STI history, hepatitis B/C, syphilis.
3. Exposed patient details: last menstrual period, contraception, emergency contraception use, pregnancy / breastfeeding plans, prior HIV testing and status, prior PrEP/PEP, hepatitis B vaccination and immunity, STI history, renal/liver disease, medications, allergies, symptoms of acute seroconversion - fever, rash, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, myalgia, headache, vomiting/diarrhea, genital ulcer/discharge.
4. Consent, safety, ongoing risk - need for condoms, partner notification, intimate partner violence screening, counseling, substance use.

Patient request despite being outside window requires shared decision-making: explain lack of benefit after 72 hours, side effects - nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, headache, fatigue, renal injury from tenofovir, hepatotoxicity, drug interactions, and that starting ART late will not abort established infection and could select resistance. Document counseling.

If she *were* within 72 hours, typical nPEP would be 28 days of tenofovir-DF + emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor such as raltegravir or dolutegravir, started urgently - do not delay for labs. That is not applicable here.

> U=U does not apply to a recently diagnosed partner not yet suppressed. Receptive vaginal intercourse risk is ~8 per 10,000 exposures if source is viremic, higher with acute HIV, STI, trauma/bleeding, menses.

### Testing to order now for the exposed 35-year-old woman

Baseline now, do not wait:

**HIV:**
* 4th-generation HIV Ag/Ab combo assay
* Consider HIV RNA PCR if acute infection suspected - symptoms, very recent high-risk exposure where Ag/Ab may still be negative, or if baseline Ag/Ab positive. RNA is not for routine screening alone.

**Pregnancy and emergency contraception assessment:**
* Urine or serum hCG
* LMP, usual contraception, time since unprotected intercourse. If within 120 hours, offer emergency contraception - copper IUD most effective, ulipristal acetate or levonorgestrel. Non-smoker status is favorable for hormonal options, social alcohol use needs counseling on adherence and liver risk but is not an absolute contraindication.

**STI screen:**
* NAAT for gonorrhea and chlamydia - vaginal swab, plus pharyngeal/rectal if indicated by sexual practices
* Trichomonas NAAT
* Syphilis serology - treponemal test + non-treponemal RPR/VDRL titer
* Hepatitis B: HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc
* Hepatitis C antibody +/- RNA if positive
* Evaluate for bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, genital lesions

**Baseline safety labs that would have been needed for PEP/PrEP, and still useful for follow-up:**
* CBC
* Serum creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis
* Liver function tests - AST/ALT, bilirubin
* Review medications for interactions

Test source if available: HIV viral load, CD4, resistance genotype, syphilis, HBsAg, HCV Ab, GC/CT.

### Follow-up and additional management

1. **HIV follow-up testing after a high-risk exposure without PEP:** repeat 4th-gen Ag/Ab at ~6 weeks, 12 weeks, and 6 months post-exposure per classic nPEP follow-up schedule; many centers now do 6 weeks and 4 months with 4th-gen assay. Repeat RNA and urgent ID referral if seroconversion symptoms develop in 2-4 weeks.
   Counsel to use condoms/abstain, not donate blood/tissue, discuss breastfeeding risk, and return promptly for fever/rash/pharyngitis/lymphadenopathy.

2. **STI follow-up:** treat if positive, re-screen in 2 weeks and 3 months for syphilis, repeat GC/CT NAAT if symptoms persist. Presumptive STI treatment is routine after sexual assault; after consensual exposure, test and treat, with low threshold for presumptive treatment if high prevalence, symptoms, or follow-up uncertain - per local STI guidelines. Doxy PEP is currently recommended by CDC only for MSM and transgender women, not routinely for cisgender women.

3. **Hepatitis B:** vaccinate if non-immune. No HBIG/PEP needed for sexual exposure unless unvaccinated with high-risk exposure - follow CDC HBV PEP guidance.

4. **Ongoing HIV prevention:** Because PEP is not an option, assess for **PrEP** if ongoing risk with a partner not yet undetectable. For receptive vaginal sex, options are tenofovir-DF/emtricitabine oral daily, long-acting injectable cabotegravir, or long-acting lenacapavir - Descovy (tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine) is *not* indicated for receptive vaginal exposure. Can discuss same-day PrEP start if baseline HIV Ag/Ab negative and no acute symptoms, with renal, pregnancy, HBV screening.

5. **Referrals:** ID/sexual health, OB-GYN/family planning, counseling, social work, partner testing and linkage to ART for source to achieve undetectable = untransmittable.

In summary: document a single unprotected receptive vaginal exposure to a likely viremic partner >72 hours ago, obtain baseline HIV Ag/Ab +/- RNA, hCG, GC/CT/trich NAAT, syphilis, Hep B panel, Hep C Ab, CBC, creatinine, LFTs, counsel that PEP is not indicated or effective after 72 hours, arrange HIV re-testing and STI follow-up, address emergency contraception if still within 120 hours, and offer PrEP and risk-reduction for ongoing risk.

This patient has **latent TB infection, not active TB** - he does not need immediate TB treatment, isolation, or work exclusion, and deferral for a few months is acceptable with counseling and a safety-net plan.

> Positive IGRA in an asymptomatic person from a TB-endemic country + normal chest x-ray + no known exposure = LTBI until proven otherwise.

LTBI is not contagious, not clinically ill, and cannot transmit to his spouse and children. Treatment is preventive, to reduce future reactivation, not urgent curative treatment.

### 1. Confirm this is LTBI and not active TB

You have already done most of the rule-out. Complete it:

**History to document:**
- TB symptoms review: cough >2-3 weeks, hemoptysis, fever, night sweats, unintentional weight loss, lymphadenopathy, bone/joint pain, headache, hematuria - he reports none
- Prior TB disease, prior LTBI treatment, adequacy and adherence, BCG history - BCG does not cause positive Quantiferon
- Timing: birth country, time in US, recent travel to endemic country, known close contact with active pulmonary TB, homeless shelter, incarceration, healthcare work
- Reactivation risks: HIV, diabetes, CKD/dialysis, silicosis, gastrectomy, TNF-alpha blocker / steroids / other immunosuppression planned, transplant, hematologic malignancy, smoking, alcohol/drug use, malnutrition
- Medications, contraception in partner - relevant for rifamycins, liver disease, peripheral neuropathy risk, drug interactions

**Exam:** vitals, weight, lung, lymph nodes, general.

**Already done:** Chest x-ray negative today for infiltrate, cavity, effusion, miliary pattern, adenopathy. No old fibronodular disease.

In an immunocompetent asymptomatic adult with normal CXR, no sputum AFB smear/culture or CT is needed. If CXR showed fibrosis, granuloma, or he was HIV-positive / severely immunosuppressed, sputum cultures would be needed even without symptoms to exclude active disease before LTBI monotherapy.

**Labs before LTBI treatment, can be done now or at treatment visit:**
- HIV test for all with LTBI, HbA1c/diabetes screen, baseline AST/ALT/bilirubin if liver disease, alcohol use, hepatotoxic meds, pregnancy risk, or age >35 if INH considered
- Hepatitis B/C if risk factors

Single positive Quantiferon in a person born in a high-prevalence country is sufficient - no confirmatory repeat needed in the absence of lab error concern.

### 2. Does he need treatment now?

No.

Active TB requires immediate airborne isolation, public health reporting, 4-drug RIPE therapy, and contact investigation. He has none of those indications.

LTBI treatment is **recommended but elective**:

- Persons born in high TB-prevalence countries are a USPSTF/CDC target group for LTBI testing and treatment because of higher prevalence of infection and reactivation risk.
- Lifetime reactivation without treatment is ~5-10%, highest in first 2 years after infection. For remote infection from country of origin, risk is lower per year but persists for life, increased by diabetes, HIV, immunosuppression, etc.
- Treatment reduces progression by 60-90%.

There is no high-urgency feature here: no symptoms, normal CXR, no recent close contact, no HIV/immunosuppression, no planned TNF-blocker/transplant, no fibrotic lesion.

Deferral for a few months is standard practice with shared decision-making, provided:

1. Document informed deferral, not refusal
2. Educate on reactivation symptoms: persistent cough, hemoptysis, fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, fatigue, swollen nodes - return promptly, repeat CXR then
3. Advise to expedite treatment if new exposure, HIV diagnosis, diabetes, or starting steroids/biologics
4. Schedule definite follow-up in 2-3 months for LTBI treatment initiation
5. Reassure: normal household life, no masks, no separate bedroom, no work restriction, no need to test spouse/children *as contacts*. If spouse/children are also from endemic country, they should have their own routine LTBI risk screening, not because of exposure to him.

### 3. With what regimen when he is ready?

Do NOT start until active TB is confidently excluded - rifampin or rifapentine alone for active TB will create resistance.

For a healthy 44-year-old adult, **short-course rifamycin-based regimens are preferred** over 6-9 months isoniazid because of higher completion, less hepatotoxicity - particularly important >35-40 years old.

CDC preferred, assuming no drug interactions, liver disease, or rifamycin contraindication:

**1. 3HP - 3 months once-weekly isoniazid + rifapentine - most commonly used:**
12 weekly doses: Isoniazid 15 mg/kg max 900 mg weekly + Rifapentine weight-based weekly, >=50 kg: 900 mg weekly. Can be self-administered with monthly monitoring. Give pyridoxine if neuropathy risk.

**2. 4R - 4 months daily rifampin:**
Rifampin 10 mg/kg max 600 mg daily x 120 doses.

**3. 3HR - 3 months daily isoniazid + rifampin:**
Isoniazid 5 mg/kg max 300 mg daily + Rifampin 10 mg/kg max 600 mg daily.

Alternative if rifamycin cannot be used: 6 months daily isoniazid 5 mg/kg max 300 mg + pyridoxine, with monthly LFT symptom monitoring.

Counseling for rifamycins: orange discoloration of tears/urine/sweat and contacts, induction of CYP450 - reduces effectiveness of combined oral contraceptives, warfarin, methadone, many antiretrovirals, anticonvulsants, etc., hepatotoxicity symptoms, rash, GI upset, flu-like reaction with intermittent rifapentine. Baseline and monthly clinical check, LFTs if baseline abnormal or risk factors.

In summary: reassure LTBI, not infectious active TB, no immediate therapy or household contact investigation needed, document plan to re-engage in a few months for 3HP or 4R after full risk assessment and labs.

This pattern - mildly elevated creatinine with normal cystatin C, bland urinalyses, normal BP, no nephrotoxins - is most often a non-GFR determinant of creatinine, not true GFR loss, but it needs confirmation and updated markers of kidney damage. This is educational information, not medical advice - he needs in-person primary care, and nephrology if abnormalities persist.

CKD by KDIGO 2024 requires persistence >3 months of:
eGFR <60 ml/min/1.73m2 OR markers of damage: albuminuria, glomerular hematuria, tubular dysfunction, histology, imaging abnormality, transplant history.

He does not meet that on current data, and a 5-year-old UACR and ultrasound are too old to rule out current damage.

For a 26 year old man, Cr 1.2 ~ eGFRcr ~85, Cr 1.4 ~ eGFRcr ~70 by CKD-EPI 2021 race-free. That is a small absolute change, within lab, hydration, diet, exercise and muscle mass variation, and does not meet AKI criteria of +0.3 in 48h or 50% in 7 days. A normal cystatin C is reassuring and KDIGO specifically recommends a confirmatory combined creatinine-cystatin C eGFR when eGFRcr is 45-59 without albuminuria, or when muscle mass, diet, or medications are suspected to bias creatinine.

Maternal grandmother with rheumatoid arthritis at age 65 does not confer hereditary kidney disease risk to him. RA can have renal complications - chronic NSAID use, secondary AA amyloidosis, rheumatoid vasculitis, methotrexate/cyclosporine toxicity - but late-onset disease in a second-degree relative is not an indication for autoimmune serologies or genetic kidney testing in an asymptomatic young adult with bland urine. What matters is family history of kidney failure, dialysis/transplant <60, polycystic kidneys, Alport - hematuria + hearing loss + eye disease, early hypertension/diabetes, recurrent stones/UTIs.

Further workup needed:

1. Focused history and exam to explain creatinine
- Trend: review all prior Cr/eGFR, same lab/assay, baseline hydration/illness at time of draws.
- Body habitus, muscle mass, BMI, weight training, recent intense exercise within 24-48h, runner/rhabdomyolysis, high protein / cooked meat meal before draw, creatine monohydrate, protein powders, anabolic steroids, TRT, diuretics.
- Full med/supplement review: NSAIDs including intermittent, PPIs, antibiotics esp trimethoprim, cimetidine, fenofibrate, antiretrovirals, lithium, herbal/supplements, alcohol, smoking, vaping, recreational drugs.
- Kidney review: foamy urine, gross hematuria, nocturia, oliguria, dysuria, flank pain, stones, UTIs, obstruction, edema, dyspnea, rash, joint pain, sinus/pulmonary symptoms, hearing/vision loss, hypertension, diabetes, gout, cardiovascular disease.
- Diabetes, hypertension, autoimmune, hepatitis B/C, HIV risk, occupational solvents/heavy metals.
- Family: specifically kidney disease, dialysis, transplant, PKD, Alport, FSGS, early HTN/diabetes, deafness.
- Vitals: repeated standardized office BP in both arms, orthostatics if indicated, weight, edema, skin rash, joint exam, muscle habitus. No edema + normal BP is reassuring but need proper technique and trend.

2. Updated labs under standardized conditions
Repeat in 2-4 weeks to 3 months, well-hydrated, avoid heavy exercise 24-48h, avoid large cooked meat meal, hold non-essential creatine/NSAIDs if clinician agrees:
- BMP with repeat creatinine + eGFRcr, cystatin C + eGFRcys and combined eGFRcr-cys CKD-EPI 2021
- UA with microscopy, not dip alone: pH, specific gravity, protein, blood, leuk esterase, nitrites, glucose, plus sediment for RBCs, RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs, WBC casts
- First-morning urine albumin-creatinine ratio, repeat 2-3x over 3 months if elevated to confirm; add urine protein-creatinine ratio if dip protein positive
- CBC, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, bicarbonate, albumin, glucose/HbA1c, lipids
- Consider CK if heavy training, TSH, CRP if cystatin interpretation in doubt - hyperthyroidism, steroids, inflammation, obesity increase cystatin; hypothyroidism, low muscle mass decrease creatinine. Normal cystatin argues against true CKD but interpret in context.

Do NOT order ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, complements, SPEP/UPEP, hepatitis panel routinely based only on grandmother's RA. Reserve for proteinuria >300-500 mg/g, glomerular hematuria with proteinuria, RBC casts, rapid eGFR fall, systemic vasculitis/lupus features, unexplained anemia, hypercalcemia, etc.

3. Imaging
Renal bladder ultrasound 5 years ago normal does not need urgent repeat if repeat UACR, UA microscopy, and combined eGFR are normal and BP remains normal. Repeat with kidney size, cortical echogenicity, hydronephrosis, cysts, stones, bladder residual if: persistent eGFRcr-cys <60, persistent UACR >30 mg/g, persistent microscopic hematuria with proteinuria, obstructive symptoms, recurrent UTIs/stones, family PKD, rapid Cr rise.

4. Resolve persistent creatinine-cystatin discrepancy
If combined eGFR is normal >60 and UACR/UA normal: no CKD, monitor in primary care.
If discrepancy persists and precise GFR matters - e.g. kidney donor evaluation, chemotherapy dosing, research - consider 24-hour urine creatinine clearance with careful collection + measured lean body mass assessment, or gold-standard measured GFR with iohexol/iothalamate via nephrology. Usually not needed first-line.

5. Follow-up and counseling
- If stable: repeat BP, BMP/eGFRcr-cys, UA, UACR in 3-6 months then annually, diabetes screening, avoid dehydration, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides if possible, maintain healthy weight, smoking cessation, adequate hydration with exercise, avoid high-dose creatine.
- Refer nephrology promptly for: eGFR <60 persistent, UACR persistently >30 mg/g, hematuria + proteinuria, RBC casts, rapid decline, resistant hypertension, electrolyte/acid-base abnormality, suspected glomerular disease, ultrasound abnormality.

Red flags needing urgent evaluation: gross hematuria, markedly foamy urine + edema, oliguria, flank pain/fever, severe headache/chest pain with very high BP, dyspnea/edema.

In short: update what is old - combined creatinine-cystatin eGFR under standardized conditions, first-morning UACR, UA with microscopy, diabetes/BP assessment, detailed muscle/diet/supplement/exercise history - and only pursue autoimmune workup or new ultrasound if those show persistent eGFR loss or kidney damage.

This pattern - persistent frequency/nocturia with dilute urine - needs to be worked up as polyuria / water diuresis, not just cystitis/UTI.

Low urine osmolality and low urine sodium point away from osmotic diuresis, salt wasting, or diuretic effect, and toward excretion of dilute, solute-poor urine: diabetes insipidus - central, nephrogenic - or primary polydipsia with appropriate renal water excretion.

Normal CMP and A1c are helpful - no overt hyperglycemia, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, or renal failure - but they do not rule out DI if thirst is intact and the patient is keeping up with water intake. Serum sodium can still be normal.

> This is general information only and not medical advice - this workup needs to be done in person, ideally with primary care + endocrinology +/- nephrology and urology.

### 1. Confirm true polyuria vs. frequency

Frequency, urgency, dysuria, small voids = storage/bladder issue.
Polyuria, polydipsia, large voids, nocturia with large volumes = water handling issue. They can co-exist.

- 3-day frequency-volume bladder diary: timing and volume of every void, every fluid intake, caffeine, alcohol, evening fluids, incontinence, urgency, nocturia episodes
- 24-hour urine collection: total volume, creatinine for completeness, osmolality, sodium, potassium, urea, glucose, protein
  - Polyuria: >3.0 L/24h or >40 mL/kg/24h
  - Nocturnal polyuria in a young adult: nighttime urine >20% of 24h volume
  - Solute excretion: Uosm x volume. >1000 mOsm/day suggests solute diuresis; <800-1000 with low Uosm suggests water diuresis
- IPSS / overactive bladder symptom scores, sleep history, snoring/apnea, edema, dyspnea, snoring, weight gain

In a 28 year old man also review: total water intake for fitness/health, energy drinks, caffeine, alcohol, smoking, anticholinergics, diuretics, lithium, valproate, demeclocycline, amphotericin, foscarnet, ifosfamide, CKD, sickle cell, prostate symptoms, STI risk, prior head trauma, neurosurgery, meningitis/encephalitis, pituitary disease, family history of DI, psychiatric history, psychogenic polydipsia.

Physical: vitals + orthostatics, weight, hydration status, edema, prostate exam, neurologic exam, visual fields if pituitary concern.

### 2. Paired blood and urine water handling labs

Get simultaneous, preferably early morning fasting:

Serum: sodium, measured osmolality by freezing-point depression *and* calculated osmolality = 2xNa + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, creatinine/eGFR, glucose, TSH, morning cortisol if pituitary concern

Urine: osmolality, sodium, potassium, glucose, specific gravity, UA + culture

Interpretation principle:
- Uosm <300 mOsm/kg, especially <100-150, = dilute urine, water diuresis. Concentrated Uosm >600-800 after overnight water restriction argues against complete DI.
- Serum Na high-normal/high + serum osm >295 + Uosm low = diabetes insipidus until proven otherwise
- Serum Na low-normal/low + serum osm <280 + Uosm low + large intake = favors primary polydipsia
- Urine glucose positive, high Uosm >300 with high solute excretion = osmotic diuresis - e.g. hyperglycemia, mannitol, high protein tube feeds, resolving AKI - already less likely with normal A1c
- Urine Na high + polyuria = diuretic, salt wasting, Bartter, etc. - less likely here with low urine Na

Also check serum calcium, potassium again, and consider PTH, vitamin D if calcium abnormal, since hypercalcemia and hypokalemia cause nephrogenic DI.

### 3. Specific test for central vs nephrogenic DI vs primary polydipsia

Do not do unsupervised water deprivation. Refer to endocrinology.

Modern standard is copeptin, the stable surrogate for ADH/vasopressin:

- Baseline copeptin >21.4 pmol/L without prior water restriction: suggests nephrogenic DI
- Hypertonic saline-stimulated copeptin: 3% saline infusion to target serum Na >150, then copeptin
  - <4.9 pmol/L = central DI
  - >4.9 pmol/L = primary polydipsia
- Arginine-stimulated copeptin is an alternative where hypertonic saline is not available

Classic water deprivation test + desmopressin challenge is less accurate but still used:
baseline weight, serum Na/osm, urine osm/volume hourly with strict monitoring, then exogenous desmopressin. Central DI concentrates urine >50% after desmopressin; nephrogenic DI does not; primary polydipsia concentrates with deprivation alone and has low baseline serum osm/Na.

### 4. If central DI is suspected

- Anterior pituitary panel: 8am cortisol/ACTH, TSH + free T4, LH, FSH, testosterone, prolactin, IGF-1
- MRI sella/brain with contrast with dedicated pituitary cuts: pituitary adenoma, stalk thickening, infiltrative disease - sarcoid, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, IgG4, germinoma, craniopharyngioma, loss of posterior pituitary bright spot, empty sella
- History: trauma, surgery, radiation, meningitis, autoimmune disease, family AVP-gene DI

If nephrogenic DI suspected: medication review and stop offending drug if possible, renal ultrasound, evaluate for CKD, obstruction, polycystic kidneys, amyloid, Sjogren, sickle cell trait/disease, chronic pyelonephritis.

### 5. Don't forget non-DI causes of frequency/nocturia in a young man

Persistent frequency after presumed UTI needs:

- Repeat UA, urine microscopy, urine culture, urine cytology if hematuria, urine glucose/protein
- STI NAAT for gonorrhea/chlamydia, trichomonas if risk, prostatitis screen - perineal pain, ejaculatory pain, boggy prostate
- Post-void residual bladder scan, uroflowmetry
- Sleep apnea screen - very common cause of nocturia: snoring, witnessed apneas, daytime sleepiness, BMI, neck circumference
- Cardiac, renal, venous insufficiency, evening diuretics, caffeine/alcohol, anxiety, overactive bladder
- Urology referral for cystoscopy/urodynamics if sterile pyuria, hematuria, obstructive symptoms, incontinence, or high residual

In practice for this patient: quantify intake/output with diary + 24h urine, get paired serum Na + measured serum osm + urine osm/electrolytes, review all fluids/drugs, screen for apnea and urologic causes, and refer to endocrinology for supervised copeptin testing +/- pituitary MRI if labs suggest central or nephrogenic DI.

New wedge infarct on CT in a 60 year old woman is never incidental - you have to find the source. Normal creatinine does not rule out important disease.

Think in 3 buckets:

1. **Cardioembolic** - most common, especially at age 60: atrial fibrillation/flutter, valvular disease, LV thrombus, endocarditis, PFO/paradoxical embolus, non-bacterial thrombotic marantic endocarditis
2. **In-situ renal artery disease / systemic vascular disease:** atherosclerotic embolus, dissection, fibromuscular dysplasia - classic in middle-aged women, vasculitis e.g. polyarteritis nodosa, Takayasu, giant cell
3. **Hypercoagulable state:** cancer-associated Trousseau, antiphospholipid syndrome, inherited thrombophilia, pro-thrombotic drugs, smoking, estrogen

Ovarian cancer history puts cancer-associated arterial thrombosis and marantic endocarditis high on the list. Family history of RA in mother does not cause renal infarct, but it raises pre-test probability for systemic autoimmunity in the patient and should prompt a full rheumatologic review.

Workup:

**1. Clarify acuity and confirm infarct**
- Review images with radiology: acute wedge-shaped perfusion defect vs chronic scar, bilateral vs unilateral, renal artery patency, aortic atheroma, adrenal/renal masses, signs of cancer recurrence, other emboli - spleen, bowel, brain
- Symptoms: onset flank/abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, fever, hematuria, oliguria, hypertensive urgency, palpitations, syncope, stroke/TIA symptoms, claudication, livedo, rash, arthralgia, sinus/pulmonary symptoms, leg swelling, dyspnea/chest pain for PE/DVT
- Vitals + exam: BP both arms and log, orthostatics, new hypertension - renin-mediated common after infarct, cardiac murmur, AFib, stigmata of endocarditis, livedo reticularis, digital ischemia, purpura, synovitis, nodules, neuropathy, temporal artery exam
- Meds: estrogen/HRT, tamoxifen, bevacizumab/anti-VEGF, cisplatin, steroids, NSAIDs, JAK-inhibitors, anticoagulant adherence, recent angiography/trauma, smoking, HTN, diabetes, dyslipidemia, migraine with aura, recurrent miscarriage, preeclampsia, prior VTE, family clot/stroke/CAD/autoimmune history
- Labs for acuity: CBC, basic metabolic panel for baseline/follow-up creatinine/eGFR, LDH - markedly elevated in acute infarct, AST/ALT, CK, urinalysis with microscopy + spot protein/creatinine - hematuria and proteinuria common, do not miss active sediment/RBC casts suggesting vasculitis/GN

**2. Cardiac embolic workup - do in all renal infarcts**
- ECG, continuous telemetry, prolonged rhythm monitoring - 14-day patch/Holter for paroxysmal AFib
- Transthoracic echo with bubble study. Low threshold for transesophageal echo given ovarian cancer history: rule out vegetation, marantic non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis, PFO, atrial septal aneurysm, LV thrombus, aortic arch atheroma
- Blood cultures x2 if fever, murmur, leukocytosis before antibiotics - to distinguish infective vs marantic endocarditis
- Fasting lipids, HbA1c, carotid imaging only if concomitant neuro symptoms or high atherosclerotic burden

**3. Renal vascular imaging**
- CTA abdomen/pelvis with arterial phase or MRA renal arteries + aorta: atherosclerosis, dissection, aneurysm/microaneurysm of PAN, beading of FMD/vasculitis, thrombus
- Renal duplex Doppler as follow-up, renal length, resistive indices
- Monitor BP closely, repeat creatinine in 48-72h and 2-4 weeks, quantify proteinuria - unilateral infarct can preserve GFR but cause new hypertension and CKD risk

**4. Hypercoagulable + oncology workup**
- Oncology review: surveillance CT already done - CA-125, exam for recurrence, review chemo history. Mucinous ovarian cancers are highly pro-thrombotic
- Lower extremity Doppler if leg symptoms, CT chest if PE symptoms - cancer patients often have concomitant VTE
- Antiphospholipid panel: lupus anticoagulant, IgG/IgM anticardiolipin, IgG/IgM beta-2 glycoprotein I - arterial infarct + autoimmunity family history + cancer association. Repeat at 12 weeks if positive
- Consider inherited workup if no clear cardioembolic/atherosclerotic cause, recurrent clots, strong family clot history: Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S/antithrombin, homocysteine, JAK2 if myeloproliferative clues, PNH screen if cytopenias. Hematology input
- Age-appropriate: no smoking, stop estrogen if acute clot, statin/diabetes/HTN optimization

**5. Autoimmune/vasculitis workup - prompted by family RA but indicated for any unexplained arterial infarct**
- ESR, CRP, ANA with reflex, ANCA - MPO/PR3, RF + anti-CCP, C3/C4, cryoglobulins, SPEP, hepatitis B/C, HIV, syphilis screen if vasculitis suspected
- Ask patient directly about inflammatory arthritis: morning stiffness >1hr, MCP/MCP swelling, sicca, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, Raynaud, sinusitis/epistaxis, hemoptysis, purpura, mononeuritis
- Rheumatology referral if positive serologies, active sediment, pulmonary-renal signs, livedo, neuropathy

Renal biopsy is not first-line for isolated wedge infarct with normal renal function and bland urine. Reserve for unexplained AKI, nephritic sediment, heavy proteinuria, or suspected small-vessel vasculitis/GN.

In practice: admit if acute pain/fever/LDH rise/hypertension, start heparin if acute infarct and no bleeding/contraindication in consultation with nephrology/cardiology/hematology, arrange ECG, prolonged monitoring, TTE +/- TEE, CTA renal arteries, UA, LDH, ESR/CRP, ANA/ANCA/APL panel, and oncology follow-up for recurrence. Then long-term BP log, repeat renal function/proteinuria, secondary prevention.

For educational purposes only - needs in-person evaluation by nephrology, cardiology, hematology, rheumatology and oncology.

This is a classic high-frequency episodic migraine phenotype, possibly a persistent post-traumatic headache with migraine phenotype.

40 year old man, 18 months of progressive left-sided headache, now 8-hour episodes 2-3 days/week = ~8-12 headache days/month, with photophobia and nausea, interfering with work, no focal deficit on exam, aborting only with aspirin/ibuprofen. History of multiple sports-related mild TBIs, never evaluated by neurology, never imaged.

Most likely: migraine without aura, high-frequency episodic, vs. persistent headache attributed to traumatic brain injury.

ICHD-3 persistent post-traumatic headache attributed to mild TBI requires headache developing within 7 days of injury and persisting >3 months. In practice many post-traumatic headaches look exactly like migraine - unilateral, pulsating, 4-72 hours, photophobia, phonophobia, nausea, worsened by activity - and are treated as migraine. Late 30s onset, strictly side-locked left pain, and progressive increase in frequency is typical of migraine chronification, but is also what makes clinicians consider secondary causes.

Other primaries are less likely:
tension-type is bilateral, pressing, no nausea/photophobia; cluster is 15-180 min with ipsilateral autonomic features and restlessness, 1-8x/day; hemicrania continua/paroxysmal hemicrania are strictly unilateral but shorter and with autonomic features and absolute indomethacin response; primary stabbing headache is seconds.

> This is educational information only, not medical advice for a specific patient. He needs in-person primary care and neurology evaluation with full neuro exam, vitals, headache diary, MIDAS/HIT-6, and screening for post-concussive comorbidities.

### Should imaging be obtained?

Routinely, no - but a one-time MRI is commonly done and reasonable here with shared decision-making.

American Academy of Neurology Choosing Wisely, American Headache Society, US Headache Consortium, and ACR Appropriateness Criteria for Headache state:

Do not routinely image stable headaches that meet criteria for migraine, have a normal neurologic exam, and have no red flags or atypical features.

Red flags - SNOOP4 + trauma:
Systemic: fever, weight loss, cancer, immunosuppression
Neurologic: focal deficit, papilledema, altered consciousness, seizure
Onset: thunderclap/worst of life
Older: new onset >50
Progressive: change in pattern, increasing severity, positional, Valsalva-induced, nocturnal awakening
History of neoplasm, anticoagulation, recent trauma

He has no focal findings, no thunderclap, no systemic symptoms per vignette. Remote sports TBIs without acute head trauma now are not an indication for emergent CT.

That is why guidelines would say: MRI head without contrast and CT head without contrast are Usually Not Appropriate for chronic stable migraine without red flags/new features.

In practice, many neurologists would still obtain a baseline MRI brain without contrast in this man because:

1. never imaged
2. late onset for new migraine - typical onset teens-20s, onset at ~38-39
3. strictly side-locked left pain
4. progressive frequency over 18 months from every few months to weekly
5. history of repetitive TBI with concern for chronic subdural hygroma/hematoma, contusion encephalomalacia, pituitary injury, vascular dissection/AVM - low yield remotely but patient and clinician reassurance
6. to exclude mimics before committing to years of preventive therapy: tumor, AVM, Chiari, sinus disease, cervical spine pathology

That is not urgent/emergent imaging. If obtained, MRI brain without contrast is preferred - no radiation, better for posterior fossa, white matter injury, hemosiderin, pituitary. CT only if MRI contraindicated/unavailable or concern for acute bleed/fracture. MRA/CTA, EEG are not indicated without thunderclap, focal deficit, or seizure.

Counsel on return precautions: sudden worst headache, focal weakness/numbness, aphasia, visual loss, seizure, syncope, fever with neck stiffness, headache with exertion/cough/sex/posture change, treatment resistance or further pattern change -> re-examine and image promptly.

### What treatments are recommended?

1. Refer to neurology/headache, keep headache diary: frequency, duration, severity, laterality, associated symptoms, triggers, menses in partner? no, sleep, caffeine, alcohol, medication use and response, work disability.

2. Education and comorbidity screen:
regular sleep, meals, hydration, aerobic exercise, stress management, limit caffeine and alcohol, avoid smoking.
Screen for depression, anxiety, PTSD, sleep apnea/insomnia, cognitive complaints, dizziness/vestibular symptoms, neck pain, substance use - all common after repetitive mTBI and migraine chronification drivers.
Counsel on head injury prevention: avoid contact/collision sports, proper return-to-play, occupational safety. Consider multidisciplinary concussion evaluation, neuropsych testing if cognitive complaints, morning cortisol/TSH/testosterone/LH/FSH/prolactin/IGF-1 if fatigue, sexual dysfunction, growth failure suggestive of post-traumatic hypopituitarism.
Assess vascular risk before triptans: BP, smoking, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, CAD, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine, pregnancy in partner? not relevant.

3. Optimize acute treatment - aspirin/ibuprofen alone is insufficient for 8-hour disabling migraine with photophobia:
First-line: early NSAID + triptan, e.g. sumatriptan 50-100 mg, rizatriptan 10 mg, eletriptan 40 mg, zolmitriptan, with antiemetic if needed e.g. metoclopramide. Avoid opioids and butalbital.
Limit use to avoid medication-overuse headache: triptans/combinations <10 days/month, simple NSAIDs/acetaminophen <15 days/month. He is at 8-12 days/month - borderline, counsel explicitly.
If triptan contraindicated, not tolerated, or fails: gepants - ubrogepant, rimegepant, zavegepant - or ditan lasmiditan. Rimegepant 75 mg can be used both acutely and every other day preventively.

4. Offer preventive therapy - indicated.
Threshold: >=4 headache days/month with disability, or >=6 days/month regardless. He has ~8-12 days/month interfering with work = high-frequency episodic migraine, strong indication.

Options, chosen by comorbidity and preference:
oral preventives: propranolol, metoprolol, candesartan, amitriptyline, venlafaxine. Topiramate and valproate are effective but often avoided as first choice after TBI because of cognitive slowing, word-finding, mood effects with topiramate, and weight gain/tremor/teratogenicity concerns with valproate.
CGRP-targeted: erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab monthly/quarterly, or oral atogepant daily, rimegepant every other day - generally well tolerated, no CNS sedation, increasingly preferred, with emerging data in persistent post-traumatic headache with migraine phenotype.
Non-pharmacologic: CBT for headache, biofeedback, relaxation training, regular aerobic exercise, physical therapy for neck, sleep CBT.

OnabotulinumtoxinA is reserved for chronic migraine >=15 headache days/month, not indicated yet.

5. Follow-up: reassess diary, disability, acute medication use, side effects at 2-3 months, titrate preventive for 2-3 months at target dose before declaring failure. If refractory, atypical, or new red flags, proceed to MRI and secondary workup.

In short: no emergent imaging required for typical migraine with normal exam, but given late-onset, side-locked, progressive course, repetitive TBI history and no prior workup, a routine MRI brain without contrast after neurology referral is defensible for reassurance. Main intervention is migraine-specific acute therapy plus disability-based preventive therapy plus behavioral management and TBI sequelae screening, with strict limits on analgesic overuse.

A 3 month history of fluctuating confusion + delusions/paranoia
after CABG in a 63 year old with no prior dementia or
primary psychiatric disease is not normal post-operative
delirium and is not ruled out by:

* oriented x3 in clinic
* grossly normal neuro exam
* non-contrast head CT 1 month ago with "no acute infarct"

Post-operative delirium after cardiac surgery is common,
especially >60, hypertension, CAD, anesthesia, bypass,
microemboli, hypoperfusion, inflammation, polypharmacy,
sleep deprivation, but it should resolve in days to weeks.

Persistence at 3 months with lucid intervals in clinic
but intermittent confusion, delusions, paranoid thinking
at home is classic for an underlying major/mild
neurocognitive disorder unmasked by surgery, not
primary late-onset psychosis.

Orientation and a routine neuro exam are insensitive
to attention, executive function, visuospatial,
memory encoding/retrieval, and fluctuation. CT without
acute infarct does not rule out strategic infarct,
chronic microvascular disease, subdural, atrophy pattern,
posterior fossa lesion, prion, NPH, etc.

Next best is a formal neurocognitive disorder workup,
starting with objective cognition + informant function,
not reassurance:

**1. Patient + informant history:**
Do not rely on patient self-report alone. Patients with
cognitive impairment lack insight and fluctuate.
Get spouse/child/caregiver separately:
- baseline cognition before CABG, education/occupation
- onset, course: stepwise, fluctuating, rapidly progressive?
- lucid intervals vs inattention, disorganized thinking
- ADLs/IADLs: meds, finances, cooking, driving, work
- visual hallucinations - well formed people/animals?
- dream enactment behavior, acting out dreams, shouting, punching in sleep - REM sleep behavior disorder
- parkinsonism, falls, syncope, orthostasis, constipation, anosmia, daytime somnolence
- depression, apathy, anxiety, agitation, aggression, sleep-wake reversal
- falls/trauma on antiplatelets/anticoagulants, alcohol, sedatives, OTCs
- full med review: anticholinergics, sedative-hypnotics, opioids, steroids, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, amiodarone, etc.
- capacity and safety: driving, cooking, wandering, weapons, finances, living alone

Fluctuating cognition + prolonged post-op delirium + visual hallucinations/delusions/paranoia at 63 is highly suspicious for Dementia with Lewy Bodies. DLB core features: fluctuating cognition/attention, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder, spontaneous parkinsonism. Severe antipsychotic sensitivity. Ask specifically and examine for rigidity, bradykinesia, rest tremor, postural instability, orthostatics.

**2. Bedside validated testing in clinic:**
- Confusion Assessment Method for delirium: acute onset/fluctuation, inattention, disorganized thinking, altered LOC
- MoCA or MMSE + clock draw, months of year backward, days of week backward for attention, Trails, verbal fluency
- PHQ-9/GDS for post-CABG depression/pseudodementia, GAD-7, sleep screen
- vitals including orthostatics, full neuro exam for subtle parkinsonism, myoclonus, aphasia, apraxia, visual fields

**3. Medical rule-out + structural imaging:**
Routine dementia labs: CBC, CMP including Na, K, Ca, glucose, renal/hepatic, TSH, B12, syphilis screen, consider ESR/CRP, ABG, UA/culture, UDS, alcohol, HIV per risk, sleep apnea screen. Review ECG/rhythm - atrial fibrillation post-CABG with emboli.

MRI brain with DWI/FLAIR/SWI/T1 volumetric preferred over CT - evaluate chronic/strategic infarct, white matter small vessel disease, subdural, atrophy pattern, hydrocephalus, Creutzfeldt-Jakob cortical ribboning if rapidly progressive. Consider MRA/carotids, echo/bubble, prolonged rhythm monitoring given CAD/CABG/vascular risk.

EEG if ongoing fluctuation/inattention to rule out non-convulsive status, triphasic waves, CJD periodic complexes. No lumbar puncture or PET routinely unless indicated.

Refer for formal neuropsychological testing to objectively quantify domains vs premorbid estimate, differentiate delirium vs mild vs major neurocognitive disorder vs primary psychotic/depressive disorder, and neurology/geriatric psychiatry/memory clinic.

Do not start dopamine-blocking antipsychotic for delusions/paranoia without DLB workup - risk of severe sensitivity, parkinsonism, NMS, mortality. If psychosis dangerous, low-dose workup in specialty setting, consider cholinesterase inhibitor responsive DLB/Parkinson dementia psychosis.

In short: normal orientation + normal exam + negative CT does not exclude cognitive impairment. Get collateral, MoCA/neuropsych testing, ADL/IADL function, depression and DLB screen, med/labs review, and MRI brain.

Yes - treat this as a high-risk, tissue-negative TIA until proven otherwise and expedite secondary prevention workup. Do not rely on DAPT + rhythm monitoring alone.

77yo man with HTN, hyperlipidemia, diabetes with sudden unilateral right arm + leg weakness for ~30 min on awakening, no face/speech involvement, negative CT head and diffusion-negative MRI brain 1 day later = clinical TIA.

ABCD2 5:
Age >=60 =1, unilateral weakness =2, duration 10-59 min =1, diabetes =1, +/- BP >=140/90 at presentation.
4-5 = moderate-high risk, ~4% 2-day, ~6-7% 7-day, ~10% 90-day stroke risk in original cohorts. 6-7 = high risk. In practice ABCD2 >=4 = high-risk TIA requiring urgent evaluation within 24-48h. He is already ~7-8 days from onset - do not delay further.

Mother with breast cancer at 72 does not change stroke management. Single post-menopausal relative is not an indication for BRCA testing in him, continue age-appropriate cancer screening.

### What you did right

No - don't keep repeating empiric azithromycin because "it helped last time." That pattern is classic for recurrent prolonged productive cough from chronic airway disease, not for repeated acute bacterial infections that are cured by a Z-pack.

>4 weeks of productive cough almost every year after a viral illness, in a 71-year-old with no prior lung diagnosis, normal CXR and clear lungs, is subacute to chronic cough that needs a diagnosis, not empiric macrolide refills.

Prior temporary relief is misleading:

1. **Natural history:** post-viral acute bronchitis / airway hyperresponsiveness improves on its own in 3-8 weeks. Improvement after antibiotics is often coincidence.
2. **Anti-inflammatory effect:** macrolides have transient anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory effects on neutrophilic airway inflammation. That can lessen cough without eradicating infection, so it recurs.
3. **Placebo / expectation:** especially with cough.

Intermittent short courses give you the risks without the proven benefit of carefully selected long-term prophylaxis.

### Why repeated azithromycin is high risk here

In a 71-year-old, repeated empiric use means:

- **Cardiac:** QT prolongation, torsades risk, especially with diuretics, antiarrhythmics, antipsychotics, fluoroquinolones, hypokalemia. Observational data of increased cardiovascular death in older adults during azithromycin exposure.
- **Ototoxicity:** reversible and sometimes irreversible hearing loss, tinnitus - age-related risk higher.
- **GI, C. difficile, drug interactions:** warfarin, statins, calcium-channel blockers, etc. LFT abnormalities.
- **Antimicrobial resistance and NTM masking:** This is critical for recurrent productive cough. Community Strep. pneumoniae, Haemophilus, Moraxella macrolide resistance is high. More importantly, macrolide monotherapy in undiagnosed nontuberculous mycobacteria - M. avium complex, M. abscessus - can induce macrolide resistance and make a curable disease incurable. Elderly with recurrent productive cough, bronchiectasis/nodular disease on CT are the at-risk group.
- **Population stewardship:** guidelines from CDC, ACCP/CHEST, GOLD, IDSA are explicit: uncomplicated acute bronchitis in an otherwise stable adult without COPD exacerbation criteria, pneumonia, pertussis should not get antibiotics.

Normal CXR and clear lungs on auscultation do not rule out the main differentials.

### What this sounds like instead

Recurrent prolonged productive cough after viral URI with normal CXR:

- chronic bronchitis / COPD - need smoking, biomass, occupational dust, secondhand history. Definition is productive cough 3 months in 2 consecutive years, but evolving chronic bronchitis often presents like this. PFTs pending are key.
- bronchiectasis - very classic: well between episodes, then viral URI triggers weeks of productive cough with change in sputum volume/purulence. CXR is often normal. Clear lungs does not exclude it. Needs high-resolution CT.
- asthma, non-asthmatic eosinophilic bronchitis, chronic rhinosinusitis with upper airway cough syndrome with throat clearing perceived as productive
- GERD / laryngopharyngeal reflux - less likely as sole cause of *productive* cough, especially since PPIs were tried without relief, but non-acid reflux can co-exist. Famotidine control of heartburn does not exclude airway reflux, but don't anchor on it.
- Others to not miss at 71: NTM infection, immunodeficiency / hypogammaglobulinemia with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic sinus disease, ACE-inhibitor, heart failure, ILD usually dry, malignancy, TB risk factors, alpha-1 if early COPD picture.

You need smoking pack-years, exposures, vaccines - influenza, pneumococcal, RSV, COVID, Tdap/pertussis history - sputum detail: daily volume, color, purulence change, hemoptysis, wheeze, dyspnea, nasal congestion, postnasal drip, throat clearing, heartburn/regurgitation/hoarseness, dysphagia, weight loss, fevers, night sweats, sinus infections, otitis, meds especially ACE-I, cardiac history, atopy, family lung disease.

### What to do instead of empiric Z-pack

1. **Don't treat the cough reflex, work up the phenotype:**
   - PFTs with pre/post bronchodilator - pending. If obstructive, assess COPD/asthma.
   - Sputum when productive: bacterial culture, and AFB smear/culture x3 if persistent, especially before any consideration of macrolide prophylaxis. CBC with eosinophils, total IgE, FeNO if asthmatic/eosinophilic disease suspected.
   - High-resolution chest CT: to rule out bronchiectasis, airway wall thickening, mucus plugging, nodules suggestive of NTM, occult mass. Strongly consider in 71-year-old with yearly prolonged productive episodes despite normal CXR.
   - Sinus evaluation, allergy history, medication review. Consider ENT if chronic rhinosinusitis.
   - Optimize GERD lifestyle measures, but if no heartburn/regurgitation and PPI non-response, look elsewhere rather than escalating acid suppression for productive cough.

2. **Reserve antibiotics for true exacerbations:**
   For COPD: increased dyspnea + increased sputum volume + increased purulence - Anthonisen criteria. For bronchiectasis: acute change in sputum purulence/volume, dyspnea, hemoptysis, fever, with sputum culture-guided therapy. Not "cough present."

3. **Prevention and airway health:**
   Smoking cessation if relevant, confirm lung cancer screening eligibility - 50-80 yr, 20 pack-year - update vaccines, hand hygiene, pulmonary referral for airway clearance techniques, hydration, nasal saline, treatment of chronic rhinosinusitis, inhaler technique if indicated.

4. **Long-term macrolide is a specialist decision, not intermittent refills:**
   Daily azithromycin 250 mg for COPD with frequent exacerbations despite optimal therapy - Albert et al NEJM 2011 - and 500 mg 3x/week for bronchiectasis with frequent exacerbations - Wong et al Lancet 2012 - reduce exacerbations in selected patients, but require: confirmed diagnosis, frequent exacerbations despite optimal inhaled therapy/airway clearance, baseline ECG QTc, audiometry, LFTs, sputum NTM exclusion, review of interactions, monitoring for hearing loss, resistance, C. difficile. Intermittent 3-5 day courses do not replicate this benefit.

Counseling point for the patient: "Azithromycin seemed to help briefly because inflammation calmed down as the virus cleared, not because it cured a bacterial infection. Each repeat course raises your risk of heart rhythm problems, hearing loss, severe diarrhea, and resistant lung infection, and it can hide the real cause like bronchiectasis or COPD. Let's get the breathing tests, sputum, and likely a CT to find why this keeps coming back, so we can prevent it rather than chase it."

Refer to pulmonology if PFTs abnormal, CT shows bronchiectasis/nodules, sputum persistently purulent, hemoptysis, weight loss, or >2-3 exacerbations/year requiring antibiotics/steroids.

In a patient with metastatic melanoma with no other options, a Grade 3 nivolumab infusion reaction is not an automatic absolute lifetime ban - but it is a **per label permanently discontinue, do not rechallenge in routine infusion center** event.

Continuation is only possible off-label as a **rapid drug desensitization after urgent allergy / oncology risk stratification, with informed consent, in a monitored inpatient setting.** Self-resolution without treatment does not make it safe.

### 1. What happened?

68F, stage IV BRAF+ melanoma on dabrafenib/trametinib, cycle 3 nivolumab 5 days ago:

end-of-infusion nausea/vomiting, cyanotic hands, diffuse rash, bradycardia then tachycardia, fluctuating BP, rigors, diarrhea, all self-resolved.

By CTCAE v5 Infusion Related Reaction:

* Grade 1-2: transient, responds to interruption/slowing, symptomatic treatment
* Grade 3: prolonged, not rapidly responsive, recurrence after initial improvement, hospitalization indicated for sequelae
* Grade 4: life-threatening, pressors/ventilatory support

This is Grade 3 by history: multisystem cutaneous + GI + cardiovascular + respiratory/vasomotor symptoms.

Opdivo USPI:

> Grade 1-2: interrupt or slow infusion rate
> Grade 3-4: permanently discontinue

That is the default. Rechallenge is off-label and must be justified by lack of alternatives, patient preference, and ability to do desensitization safely.

Differentiate:

1. **Cytokine-release / non-IgE infusion reaction to fully human IgG4** - most common with nivolumab, <5% any grade, <1% grade 3-4. Typically rigors, fever, nausea, vomiting, rash, dyspnea, hypo/hypertension, tachycardia, dizziness during or within hours of infusion, more common early but sensitization can occur by cycle 3 with anti-drug antibodies.
2. **IgE-mediated anaphylaxis / mast-cell degranulation** - rapid flushing, urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, cyanosis, tachy then bradycardia, hypo/hypertension, GI cramping, diarrhea, nausea/vomiting. Does not require epinephrine to qualify.
3. **Immune-related adverse event, not infusion reaction** - e.g. ICI-colitis diarrhea, ICI-dermatitis, ICI-myocarditis with arrhythmia. Desensitization does NOT apply to irAEs, SJS/TEN, DRESS, pneumonitis, hepatitis, nephritis, encephalitis. Those are permanent discontinuation.
4. **Other drug / comorbidity** - dabrafenib/trametinib pyrexia syndrome with chills, rash, GI upset, hypotension; seizure meds; sepsis; carcinoid; pheochromocytoma; acute coronary syndrome with Kounis allergic vasospasm in a 68-year-old with unstable vitals; underlying clonal mast cell disease.

Scattered lentigines on sun-exposed skin in a 68-year-old are most often benign solar lentigines / melanoma risk marker, but do not dismiss:

* rule out cutaneous metastases, drug rash residua
* rule out maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis / urticaria pigmentosa mimicking lentigines, especially with flushing + hypotension + tachycardia + diarrhea + nausea. Check Darier's sign, dermatology review, biopsy if atypical.

In other words: this phenotype - cutaneous + cardiovascular lability + GI mediator symptoms triggered by a monoclonal antibody - mandates mast-cell workup before any rechallenge.

### 2. Can she continue if there are no alternatives? Conditional yes.

Published experience with PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors - nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, durvalumab - shows successful 12-step 3-bag and 16-step 4-bag rapid drug desensitization with temporary tolerance, requiring repeat desensitization each cycle.

Criteria to consider it:

* Reaction was infusion reaction / hypersensitivity, NOT SJS/TEN, DRESS, serum sickness, vasculitis, pneumonitis, colitis, hepatitis, myocarditis, neurologic irAE
* No uncontrolled asthma, cardiac ischemia, severe pulmonary hypertension that makes hypotension unsurvivable
* Allergy/immunology, oncology, pharmacy, ICU, dermatology available
* Patient understands risk of recurrent life-threatening anaphylaxis, cardiac arrest, death despite desensitization, and alternative of best supportive / targeted-only / trial / palliative care
* Family wish to proceed documented with goals-of-care discussion

If those are met, do NOT give dose 4 in <2 weeks in community clinic. Admit for planned desensitization.

### 3. Urgent workup in the next days

You have missed the acute tryptase window - 1-3 hr peak, baseline at 24hr - but still do:

* Full infusion record: dose, rate, lot, premeds, vitals flow sheet, concomitant dabrafenib/trametinib timing, seizure meds, new foods, latex, chlorhexidine
* Now: baseline serum tryptase, total IgE, CBC, CMP, troponin, ECG, consider echo if arrhythmia/chest symptoms, stool studies if diarrhea persists to exclude ICI-colitis / infection
* Mast cell screen: baseline tryptase, 24-hr urine N-methylhistamine / prostaglandin D2 / LTE4, hereditary alpha-tryptasemia TPSAB1 copy number if tryptase >8, KIT D816V if tryptase elevated or Darier positive. Dermatology for skin lesions.
* Allergy testing: skin prick with undiluted nivolumab 10 mg/mL, then intradermal 1:1000, 1:100, 1:10, with histamine/ saline controls; basophil activation test if available; anti-nivolumab antibodies where available. Negative skin test does not exclude reaction - non-IgE reactions are often skin-test negative but still desensitizable.
* Medication review: dabrafenib/trametinib hold? Usually continue unless pyrexia suspected. Check QT, LVEF, ocular toxicity. Check enzyme-inducing anti-seizure drugs - carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital - for interaction with steroids/antihistamines and for own hypersensitivity risk.
* Update allergy list, FDA MedWatch / institutional pharmacovigilance report, oncology documentation, medical alert education.

Cardiology review for bradycardia/tachycardia + fluctuating BP + cyanosis in elderly: rule out Kounis syndrome, arrhythmia, orthostatic collapse.

### 4. How desensitization is done if you proceed

Not a slower infusion alone. Example framework - must be protocolized by allergy:

* Tertiary center, 1:1 nursing, continuous telemetry, pulse oximetry, BP q15min, IV access x2, crash cart, epinephrine IM/IV, H1/H2 blockers, steroids, bronchodilators, fluids, ICU transfer plan. Prolonged observation 4-6+ hr post.
* Premedication 30-60 min before: e.g. cetirizine/diphenhydramine + famotidine + acetaminophen +/- montelukast +/- aspirin if mast-cell phenotype and no bleeding risk. Corticosteroid e.g. methylprednisolone is often used for desensitization but may blunt ICI efficacy - use lowest effective dose, discuss with oncology, avoid chronic steroids.
* 3-bag 12-step or 4-bag 16-step: start ~1:1000 to 1:100 dilution, doubling doses q15-20 min over 4-6 hr to full cumulative dose. Any breakthrough symptoms: stop, treat, then resume at prior tolerated step after stabilization.
* Tolerance is temporary - premedication + desensitization required for EVERY future cycle.
* Do not switch to pembrolizumab routinely to "avoid" allergy - same PD-1 class, high cross-reactivity risk. Switch to ipilimumab CTLA-4 or other class only as separate oncology decision with its own allergy risk, not as a safe substitute.

If breakthrough Grade 3-4 during desensitization, abort and permanently discontinue.

### 5. Counseling

> Per label we should stop nivolumab permanently. Because you have BRAF-targeted therapy resistance/progression and no other systemic options, and because this was an infusion hypersensitivity and not a severe skin, lung, colon, liver or heart immune toxicity, some centers will attempt to give it again using a desensitization procedure that induces temporary tolerance. It lowers but does not eliminate risk of another severe reaction, including death. It requires hospital admission, allergy specialists, and repeat procedure each time.

Document informed consent, code status, seizure action plan - antihistamines/sleep deprivation/stress can lower threshold - and provide anaphylaxis action plan, epinephrine autoinjector, 24-hr contact.

In short: do not rechallenge routinely; refer urgently to allergy/immunology + melanoma oncology + dermatology +/- cardiology for mast-cell and cardiac workup, and if no contraindicating irAE/SJS/DRESS and patient accepts risk, schedule inpatient rapid drug desensitization for the dose due in <2 weeks, not outpatient re-infusion.
